```{r library}
library(UTRunway)
```

## The problem

You have designed several candidate mRNA constructs. Each is the same
protein-coding sequence wrapped in a different pair of untranslated
regions, and you can afford to synthesise and test only a few of them.
Which ones?

The untranslated regions are where much of that decision sits. A 5' UTR
carrying an upstream AUG can divert scanning ribosomes away from the
real start codon. A 3' UTR carrying AU-rich elements recruits the
machinery that shortens a transcript's life. A missing polyadenylation
signal is a problem on its own. None of this requires sequencing data
to see: it is in the sequence you already have.

UTRunway reads candidate constructs, measures those features, draws
each design as a map, and ranks the candidates against one another so
that the shortlist is a decision you can explain rather than a hunch.

This vignette walks the whole workflow on the package's bundled data.
Read the **Scope and interpretation** section at the end before you
trust any number here: it says plainly what this package can and
cannot tell you.

## Reading constructs

A construct is three sequences: a 5' UTR, a coding sequence, and a
3' UTR. `readConstruct()` takes them from a data frame or from a FASTA
file, checks them, and returns a validated object everything else in
the package can rely on.

The package ships an example FASTA with one record per region:

```{r fasta-head}
fasta_path <- system.file(
  "extdata", "exampleConstructs.fasta",
  package = "UTRunway"
)
cat(head(x = readLines(con = fasta_path), n = 4), sep = "\n")
```

```{r read-fasta}
from_fasta <- readConstruct(x = fasta_path)
from_fasta[, c("construct_id", "has_ambiguous")]
nchar(x = from_fasta$utr5)
```

Reading from a data frame works the same way. The bundled
`simulatedConstructs` dataset holds twelve candidates, so we will use
six of them from here on:

```{r read-frame}
data(simulatedConstructs, package = "UTRunway")
candidates <- readConstruct(x = simulatedConstructs[1:6, ])
class(x = candidates)
```

Validation is strict and the errors name the construct at fault. All
problems are reported together, so a file with several mistakes takes
one run to diagnose rather than one run per mistake:

```{r validation-error, error = TRUE}
readConstruct(
  x = data.frame(
    construct_id = c("bad_frame", "no_start"),
    utr5 = c("GCCACC", "GCCACC"),
    cds = c("ATGGCCTA", "GGGGCCTAA"),
    utr3 = c("AATAAA", "AATAAA")
  )
)
```

## Profiling

`profileConstruct()` runs every feature function over every region of
every candidate and returns one tidy table. That table is the single
input to every plotting function and to the ranking.

```{r profile}
features <- profileConstruct(constructs = candidates)
dim(x = features)
head(x = features, n = 6)
```

Each row is one feature value for one construct. Rows with a
`position` are individual occurrences, such as a single upstream AUG;
rows without one are summaries for the region.

```{r summaries}
subset(
  x = features,
  subset = construct_id == "CONSTRUCT_03" &
    region == "utr5" & is.na(position),
  select = c(feature, value)
)
```

The `region` column is what keeps the coding sequence out of scoring
later. Everything that may contribute to a score is the rows where
`region` is not `"cds"`:

```{r regions}
table(features$region)
```

## Looking at one construct

The feature table is complete but hard to read. `plotConstructMap()`
draws one candidate on a single coordinate axis, with each class of
feature on its own labelled row.

```{r map, fig.height = 5.2}
plotConstructMap(
  feature_table = features, construct_id = "CONSTRUCT_03"
)
```

Reading the figure: CONSTRUCT_03 carries three upstream AUGs in its
5' UTR, two of which open upstream reading frames that terminate
before the coding sequence begins. Those compete with the real start
codon. The polyadenylation signal is present and sits near the 3' end,
where it belongs. The lower track is the structure proxy, discussed
below.

Compare that with a candidate whose problem is at the other end:

```{r map-12, fig.height = 5.2}
all_features <- profileConstruct(constructs = simulatedConstructs)
plotConstructMap(
  feature_table = all_features, construct_id = "CONSTRUCT_12"
)
```

CONSTRUCT_12 has a clean 5' UTR, so no rows appear for it, but its
3' UTR carries three clusters of AU-rich element pentamers and a miRNA
seed match site. Two candidates, two quite different reasons to worry.

Coding sequence features are left out by default, because nothing in
the coding sequence is ever scored. Ask for them when you want to
check the coding sequence itself:

```{r map-cds, fig.height = 5.6}
plotConstructMap(
  feature_table = features,
  construct_id = "CONSTRUCT_03",
  show_cds_context = TRUE
)
```

The two added rows are grey and named as context. CONSTRUCT_03 turns
out to carry a premature stop codon. Nothing scores it, and it would
still end the construct's usefulness, which is why the option exists.

## Comparing candidates

`plotCandidateComparison()` puts every candidate across every feature
at once. Each feature is scaled so that 0 is the lowest value in the
set and 1 the highest.

```{r comparison, fig.height = 4.8}
plotCandidateComparison(
  feature_table = features,
  highlight = c("CONSTRUCT_03", "CONSTRUCT_06")
)
```

A high point is the largest value **among these candidates**, which is
good for a canonical polyadenylation signal and bad for upstream AUGs.
Direction belongs to scoring, not to this figure. Candidates are grey
unless named in `highlight`, which takes at most three.

## Ranking

`rankCandidates()` scales each feature across the candidates, orients
it so that higher is always better, and takes a weighted mean.

```{r rank}
ranking <- rankCandidates(feature_table = features)
ranking
```

The object carries more than the order. `contributions` holds the part
each feature played in each score, which is what makes a ranking
explainable:

```{r contributions}
leader <- ranking$ranking$construct_id[[1]]
head(
  x = subset(
    x = ranking$contributions,
    subset = construct_id == leader,
    select = c(feature, value, normalised, contribution)
  ),
  n = 5
)
```

`plotScoreBreakdown()` shows all of that at once:

```{r breakdown, fig.height = 4.6}
plotScoreBreakdown(ranking = ranking)
```

Each bar is a candidate's score split into the features behind it. The
dashed rule is the most that region could contribute, so the gap
between a bar and the rule is what the candidate gave away.
CONSTRUCT_03 gives away almost the whole 5' UTR contribution, which is
the three upstream AUGs showing up as a number.

Weights are yours to choose, and they are recorded in the result so a
ranking can always be traced back to them:

```{r weights}
round(x = ranking$weights, digits = 3)
```

Naming a few features ranks on those alone:

```{r custom-weights}
rankCandidates(
  feature_table = features,
  weights = c(n_upstream_orf = 2, kozak_score_scaled = 1)
)$ranking
```

## Checking robustness

A ranking under weights you chose is worth only as much as its
stability under weights you might have chosen instead.
`rankStability()` re-ranks under many perturbed weightings and
`plotCandidateRanking()` draws the spread.

```{r stability, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(seed = 2024)
stability <- rankStability(feature_table = features, n = 200)
plotCandidateRanking(stability = stability)
```

Read the bars before the order. A candidate holding first place across
nearly every weighting is a genuinely strong candidate within this
set. A candidate whose bar spans half the field has no settled
position, and calling it third-best would be reading precision that is
not there.

```{r stability-summary}
stability$summary
```

Exploring the weight space more widely widens the bars, which is the
honest picture of how much the order depends on a choice nobody
measured:

```{r stability-wide, fig.height = 4.2}
set.seed(seed = 2024)
plotCandidateRanking(
  stability = rankStability(
    feature_table = features, n = 200, concentration = 2
  )
)
```

## Scope and interpretation

Read this section before using any number this package produces.

### Coding sequence features are context, never scored

UTRunway ranks on 5' UTR and 3' UTR features alone. `profileCDS()`
reports GC content, GC3, premature in-frame stop codons and
out-of-frame ATGs, and `plotConstructMap()` can draw them, but no
coding sequence feature reaches any score. The scope of this package
is untranslated region design: choosing the UTRs to put around a
coding sequence that has already been chosen.

There is deliberately no codon adaptation index here, no tRNA
adaptation index, and no codon usage table. For codon usage analysis
and codon optimisation, use the **cubar** package on CRAN
(<https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=cubar>), described in Liu, M.,
Zi, B., Zhang, H. and Zhang, H. (2025), "cubar: a versatile package
for codon usage bias analysis in R", *Genetics*, iyaf191.

### The structure measure is a proxy, not folding

`estimateStructure()` reports sliding-window GC content and the
longest pair of reverse-complementary runs that could pair within each
window. That is all it does. There is no nearest-neighbour energy
model, no partition function, no minimum free energy and no base pair
probability anywhere in the package.

What follows: interactions spanning more than one window are invisible
however stable they would be, a stem of A-U pairs counts the same as
one of G-C pairs, and a possible pairing is not a pairing that forms.
Use it to compare candidates against one another on the same settings.
If you need a structure prediction, fold the sequence with a
thermodynamic folding program, which is outside this package by
design, since UTRunway depends on nothing beyond R.

### The bundled data is simulated

**`simulatedConstructs` is synthetic.** Its sequences were drawn from
a uniform random base composition and then had motifs spliced into
them under a fixed random seed. They are not derived from any real
transcript, and no measured expression, translation or stability
outcome is attached to any of them.

That has a hard consequence for what this vignette demonstrates. The
bundled data can show that the detection functions find the features
that were planted: that `findUpstreamORFs()` recovers exactly the
upstream AUGs put into a sequence, that `scanDecayElements()` counts
the AU-rich pentamers that were placed there, that a disrupted
polyadenylation signal is reported as absent. Those are real tests
with known answers, and the package's test suite checks them.

**It cannot show that the scores predict anything.** Nothing in this
package has been compared against measured translation efficiency,
measured transcript stability, or tissue targeting. The ranking is a
weighted sum of normalised sequence features, with directions drawn
from published sequence determinants and weights chosen by the user.
That is a design heuristic for narrowing a candidate list. It is not a
model of outcome, and **UTRunway makes no claim that a higher-ranked
construct will perform better experimentally.**

### How such a claim could be evaluated

The claim is testable, and the way to test it is with a published
dataset that pairs sequences with measured outcomes.

One suitable dataset is the massively parallel reporter assay of
Sample et al. (2019), which measured ribosome loading across a large
library of human 5' UTRs: Sample, P. J., Wang, B., Reid, D. W.,
Presnyak, V., McFadyen, I. J., Morris, D. R. and Seelig, G. (2019),
"Human 5' UTR design and variant effect prediction from a massively
parallel translation assay", *Nature Biotechnology* 37, 803-809.

An evaluation would profile those UTRs with `profileConstruct()`,
score them with `rankCandidates()` under a fixed weighting, and
correlate the scores against the measured ribosome loading on
sequences held out of any tuning, reporting the correlation and its
confidence interval. A weighting fitted on the training portion could
be compared against the equal weighting this package defaults to, to
see whether the chosen directions carry real signal. Comparable 3' UTR
datasets measuring transcript stability would test the other half of
the score.

**This validation has not been performed.** Until it is, treat the
ranking as a way of making sequence features explicit and comparable,
not as a prediction.

## Where to go next

```{r functions, echo = FALSE}
data.frame(
  `Function` = c(
    "readConstruct", "profileConstruct", "findUpstreamORFs",
    "scoreKozak", "estimateStructure", "scanDecayElements",
    "scanMotifs", "profileCDS", "rankCandidates", "rankStability"
  ),
  `Purpose` = c(
    "Read and validate candidate constructs",
    "Profile every construct into one tidy table",
    "Locate upstream AUGs and upstream ORFs",
    "Score a start codon's initiation context",
    "Sliding-window GC and a complementarity proxy",
    "PolyA signals, AU-rich elements, miRNA seed sites",
    "Scan for built-in or supplied IUPAC motifs",
    "Coding sequence context, never scored",
    "Rank candidates with per-feature contributions",
    "How far the ranking moves with the weights"
  ),
  check.names = FALSE
)
```

Every function's help page gives its references and its limitations.
`?simulatedConstructs` documents what was planted in the bundled data
and how it was generated.

sessionInfo()
